s06.slug: FRIDAY · 6:00 PM · PICACHO PEAK, A TRUCK STOP OFF I-10 — THE CALL
body: The sun is going down behind Picacho Peak. From the pump island the mountain has gone to a cutout of itself, a black crown of rock with the light coming around its edges, and the sky over it runs orange at the bottom and red above that, and straight overhead it’s already blue. On the slope below, the saguaros stand in the last of the light with their arms up. Out on the interstate the trucks gear down for the exit one after another, a long falling groan of engine and then the gasp of the air brakes, and the wind comes across the flat with diesel in it, and hot asphalt giving back the day, and something green and resinous out in the scrub that Ohio never taught him the name of.

GAS AT HALF A TANK, NOT A QUARTER is laminated on the dash, and the gauge said half at Casa Grande, so here they are. Theo, who drove them in, has never pumped gasoline. He stands at the pump holding the nozzle in both hands with its business end pointed at the Odyssey from a respectful distance, and Kevin stands beside him with the squeegee out of the bucket, dripping on his shoes. “In the hole. Push it in. Now the handle.” Theo looks at the nozzle. “The handle. *The handle*, Theo.”
The pump starts. Theo goes still all over and watches the dollars on the display go round a good deal faster than the gallons. “Kevin,” he says. “It’s *loud*.”

Margot comes out of the store with a stick of jerky in a paper sleeve and a postcard of a saguaro, and holds her free hand out for the keys, and Theo, without letting go of anything, gets them into it. Laney is on the curb under the store’s awning in her sunglasses, one leg out straight in front of her, reaching for the toe of her boot and saying *ow* at intervals. In the open side door of the way-back Lena sits with the legal pad on her knee and the day’s receipts under its clip, writing.

The RAZR goes off in his shirt pocket, against his chest. On the little outside screen: SKYE (MISFIT). He has it open before the second ring, and leans back against the van with his free hand up on the roof rail, still warm from the sun.
“I’ve been met,” Skye says. No hello. “At the bottom of the escalator. A man in a fleece, holding a sign, and the sign said CASSIE.”
“Did you go to him?”

“Almost didn’t. I stood at the top and thought, good, she’s got a ride.” Paper rustles on her end, close to the phone. “I’ve never been met by my *character* before. I didn’t know what to say to him. I said, ‘She’s running late.’ He drove me anyway.”
Jack laughs into the wind. “How’s Burnaby?”
“Kansas with Starbucks.” Behind her a man is calling out a scene number. “Landed by lunch. Wardrobe by two. And Jack. Wardrobe went through my bags.”
“And?”

“They found your shirt. The costume lady held it up by the shoulders and said, *Whose is this*, and I said a boy’s, and she said *obviously*. They’re keeping the salsa on the cuff. They say it’s character. It got the part. It’s recurring. Cassie wears it in the porch scene, over the cardigan, with the sleeves down over her hands.” She lowers her voice, in a trailer in Canada, for him. “I wore you all afternoon. Wardrobe thinks I’m method.”
Jack looks down at the concrete of the pump island, at an old dark stain on it the shape of Lake Erie, and the back of his neck goes hot in the wind. “Is it method?”

“It’s extremely method. Ask my elbows.” She does Corinne down the line from Burnaby, consonants and all. “*Skye.* The skin person called the hotel. About your *elbows*. Cassie has *indoor* elbows. Are those *indoor* elbows?” And she’s herself again. “They’re outdoor elbows, Jack. I’ve been surfing on them. There’s going to be a meeting.”
“What about the geese?”
“The geese are real. I was right. Labradors. There was one by the stages this morning, standing on a parking bumper, and it watched me the entire way to the door like it had read the sides.”
“Did it have notes?”
“One note. It was *hiss*.”
“Pop says tell the TV one Ma says Canada’s cold.”
“The TV one.” She tries it in her mouth. “I’m going to be the TV one on Glenwood Avenue for the rest of my life, aren’t I.”
“Pretty much.”

“Good. It’s eight degrees. I have a coat she’d approve of. It’s long, and it has a lining.” The rustle again, and a long creak, somebody sitting down on something that doesn’t want her to. “I’m in a trailer. It says CASSIE on the door, so I’m subletting. I have a space heater and the sides and a cup of tea that tastes like a hotel. I’m tired, Jack. Actually tired. It’s the good kind. I haven’t had it in a while.”
“Six a.m. call tomorrow,” she says. “I’m the one with the call time now.”
Jack’s hand tightens on the roof rail.
“Where are you?” she says. “Don’t say Texas. You’re not in Texas.”
“Arizona.”
“Close enough for a margin. Read me a rude one.”

Hale’s *Moviegoer* comes out of his back pocket one-handed. It falls open where the print is, lying face-down between the pages with its back to the sky, and he keeps his thumb on it and pages on past with his other fingers to a passage where Binx is talking about making money, and about how much he enjoys it. Beside it in the margin is Hale’s small upright pencil.
“Okay,” he says. “A margin. Binx, on the subject of money.” And he reads it out across a pump island in Pinal County: “*Spoken like a man who has never paid for anything.*”
She laughs. It comes down the line out of Canada with the sound left in, hoarse at the edges from the day, and behind it he can make out the fan of a space heater in a trailer in Burnaby.
“He’s right,” she says, when she has her breath. “He’s right, and it’s a terrible note. You can’t play a man who’s never paid for anything. You can only play one who thinks the bill hasn’t come yet.”
“That should go in under his.”
“In pen. Initialed.”

Around him the truck stop does its best not to listen. Theo holds the handle in and watches the dollars. Kevin does the windshield top to bottom in long strokes and moves around to the side glass. Margot reads the back of her own postcard. Laney has her forehead down on her knee. At the side door the pen has stopped.
“Okay,” Skye says. “Tell Kevin sixty-five.”
“He knows.”
“Tell him anyway. Tell Margot I’ve started her notes. Tell Theo —” She thinks about it. “Ted. *Behave*.”
Outside her trailer a woman’s voice calls for Cassie. “That’s me,” Skye says. “I mean that’s her. I have to go be indoors.”

choices.key: At a truck stop under Picacho Peak Skye called from Burnaby, and you read her one of Hale’s rude margins at the pump. You told her you love her, in front of everybody.
response: “Love you,” he says.

He says it at the volume he says everything else, at a pump island in Arizona with five people inside twenty feet of him, and doesn’t lower it for any of them. “Say it in Texas too,” Skye says. “Bye, Pair Forty-one.”
The hinge of the RAZR complains as it shuts. He puts the phone back in his shirt pocket and gives the stop its messages in order, down the island. “Kevin. Sixty-five.”
Kevin, the squeegee up against the side glass: “*Not sixty-six.*”
“Margot. She’s started your notes.”
Margot is in the driver’s seat with the door open and the jerky in her teeth. She takes it out to say, “Tell her I’ll be the judge.”
“Theo. Ted. Behave.”
Theo gets the nozzle back into its cradle on the third try and steps away from it. “Callender has never once told me to behave and meant it.”
On the curb Laney brings her sunglasses down her nose, and over the top of them she looks at Jack until Margot turns the key; and behind him the van’s slide doors roll shut, one after another.

choices.text: “Tell Cassie she can keep the shirt.”
choices.key: At a truck stop under Picacho Peak Skye called from Burnaby, and you read her one of Hale’s rude margins at the pump. You told her Cassie can keep the shirt.
response: “Tell Cassie she can keep the shirt.”

“Hang on.” Her mouth goes away from the phone, and he hears her say it to the trailer, gravely, and wait. She comes back. “She says she will. She says it’s the warmest thing in the trailer.” The voice outside calls again. “Bye, Pair Forty-one.”

The RAZR is still warm in his hand when he leans down to the driver’s window, where Margot has the seat run up to the wheel and every mirror already wrong for everyone but her. He gives her the news through the window. “She’s started your notes.”
Margot slots the postcard into the visor. “Tell her I’ll be the judge.”
Across the hood Kevin sets the squeegee to the windshield and raises his eyebrows at Jack, and Jack says, “Sixty-five.”
“*Not sixty-six*,” Kevin says through the glass.
“Theo. Ted says behave.”
Theo gets the nozzle back into its cradle on the third try. “Callender has never once told me to behave and meant it.”
Laney’s sunglasses come down. She looks at him over them from the curb, and gets up, and dusts off the back of her jeans; and the slide doors go behind him, one and then the other.

choices.text: “I miss you. It’s been eleven hours.”
choices.key: At a truck stop under Picacho Peak Skye called from Burnaby, and you read her one of Hale’s rude margins at the pump. You told her you miss her. Eleven hours. Eleven and a half, she said.
response: “I miss you. It’s been eleven hours.”

“Eleven and a half,” she says at once. “I’m counting the airport.” Under the heater’s fan he hears her breathe out, the long one people do at the end of a day. “Me too. Go get in your van. Bye, Pair Forty-one.”
Kevin is already waiting at the end of the island when the RAZR shuts, the squeegee in his fist. “Did she say sixty-five?”
“She said sixty-five.”
“*Not sixty-six.*” Kevin drops the squeegee in the bucket. “What else?”
“Margot, she’s started your notes.”
Margot, behind the wheel with the door open, is getting her jerky out of its sleeve. “Tell her I’ll be the judge.”
“And Ted’s to behave.”
Theo gets the nozzle back into its cradle on the third try. “Callender has never once told me to behave and meant it.”
On the curb Laney’s sunglasses come down, and she looks at him over them while Kevin counts heads; and the doors of the van slide and bang shut behind him, one after another.
